call_overview.title: About the call
call_overview.question: What does the call offer, and who can apply?

cards.title: What the call wants
cards.question: What is the principal thing the project must develop, and which problem or need must it address?
cards.answer:
Innovations that cut the carbon footprint of energy-intensive process industries by at least 20% through renewable process energy, storage and energy management.
Process industries are sectors such as chemicals, steel, cement and paper that need large amounts of heat. Proposals should address several of these:
- renewable energy in production processes with better energy efficiency
- integrated energy systems with novel storage that keep plants running smoothly despite fluctuating renewable supply
- solutions for low and medium temperatures (100–500 °C), including hybrid solutions that progressively reduce fossil fuels
- solutions for high temperatures (above 500 °C), including electricity-driven processes and high-temperature storage
- high-performance insulation and innovative advanced materials for heat capture, storage and retrieval, using few critical raw materials and recyclable
Pure demand-side management, adjusting production schedules to renewable supply, is outside the scope. The need originates with industry, which must decarbonise while renewable electricity fluctuates in availability and price.
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, Digital, Industry and Space · pp. 67–70 · HORIZON-CL4-2027-02-MAT-PROD-32-two-stage, Expected Outcome and Scope

cards.title: Project impact
cards.question: Which wider system outcomes and impacts must the project support?
cards.answer:
Projects should deliver significant, broadly applicable and economically viable decarbonisation of industrial processes, with at least a 20% CO2 reduction.
- Significant reduction of greenhouse-gas emissions from the overall system
- A shift away from fossil energy for low and medium heat demands (renewable alternatives and heat upgrading) and for high-temperature processes (electrified and hybrid processes, high-temperature storage)
- A boost to clean energy use through advanced materials, system concepts and storage, supporting resilience against energy supply variations
- Combined energy savings and integrated management of energy systems and production processes
Proposals should also show how they strengthen the European supply chain for industrial decarbonisation technologies and outline societal, environmental and workplace implications.
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, Digital, Industry and Space · pp. 67–70 · HORIZON-CL4-2027-02-MAT-PROD-32-two-stage, Expected Outcome and Scope

cards.title: Who it suits
cards.question: Who may lead, which partners must take part, and how must the work be shared?
cards.answer:
Industry-led consortia of at least three independent organisations from three countries, with process-industry plants, technology suppliers and materials researchers.
- Lead: any beneficiary may coordinate; the call reserves the role for no organisation type
- Composition: the general rule requires three independent legal entities, one in an EU Member State and two others in different Member States or countries associated with Horizon Europe (non-EU countries taking part in the programme); the call names no required partner types, but the business case must be backed by the management of the companies involved
- Work split: none prescribed; as a lump sum grant, the budget is split over work packages in a detailed table at stage 2
- Exclusion: legal entities established in China are not eligible for innovation actions
The call suits energy-intensive industrial companies, suppliers of heat pumps, electric heating, boilers and thermal storage, materials developers and research institutes.

cards.title: Innovation
cards.question: How new must the project be, and in what must it innovate?
cards.answer:
The project must deliver technological innovations with a significant decarbonisation step, including new advanced materials and storage concepts; it is not limited to applying existing solutions.
The innovation combines technology (electrified, hybrid and renewable heat, storage, insulation and advanced materials) with system integration and energy management. For materials, the proposal must address the gaps from materials design to deployment, with feedback loops and early attention to scalability and industrial requirements.
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, Digital, Industry and Space · pp. 67–70 · HORIZON-CL4-2027-02-MAT-PROD-32-two-stage, Expected Outcome and Scope

cards.title: Maturity
cards.question: Which maturity level is expected at the start and end of the project?
cards.answer:
Activities are expected to start at TRL 4–5 and reach TRL 6–7 by the end of the project.
TRL 4–5 is technology validated in a laboratory or relevant environment; TRL 6–7 is demonstration in a relevant environment up to a system prototype in an operational environment.
cards.sources:

cards.title: Demonstration and integration of work
cards.question: Where must the solution be demonstrated, and how must the work fit with existing systems?
cards.answer:
Pilot-scale demonstrations are required, preferably in real industrial environments, to validate the technologies under real-world industrial conditions.
The solutions must integrate energy supply, storage and production processes so plants operate smoothly despite variable renewable supply, and tailor the capture, storage and management of energy flows to the needs of the process industry.
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, Digital, Industry and Space · pp. 67–70 · HORIZON-CL4-2027-02-MAT-PROD-32-two-stage, Scope

call_overview.title: Relevance to TenneT
call_overview.question: Why is this call relevant to TenneT?

cards.title: Why it matters to TenneT
cards.question: Why does this call matter to TenneT, and why can't TenneT take part itself?
cards.answer:
Electrifying industrial heat raises demand for grid connections and capacity; on-site storage could make that demand more flexible and ease congestion near industrial clusters.
This is our interpretation. TenneT's Onshore and Offshore Grid Investment Plans 2026 and Target Grid 2045 must accommodate industrial electrification, and the call's thermal storage and hybrid solutions could reduce peak loads. TenneT cannot usefully take part: the call funds process technology and materials pilots at industrial sites, explicitly excludes pure demand-side management, and sets out no role for a transmission system operator.
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, Digital, Industry and Space · pp. 67–70 · HORIZON-CL4-2027-02-MAT-PROD-32-two-stage, Scope

funding_timing_submission.title: Funding
funding_timing_submission.question: How much funding can the project receive?

cards.title: Funding envelope
cards.answer:
About 6 projects of EUR 7–9 million each are expected, within a topic budget of EUR 52.5 million.
- Total project size: not stated
- Grant request: EUR 7–9 million per project, for the whole consortium; other amounts may be requested and selected
- Funding form: lump sum (a fixed amount set from a detailed budget and paid against completed work packages rather than reported costs)
Final budgets may change by up to 20% after evaluation.
cards.sources:
Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, Digital, Industry and Space · pp. 20–21 · Call INDUSTRY-two-stage (HORIZON-CL4-2027-02-two-stage), Overview of this call

cards.title: Funding rate and co-financing
cards.answer:
Companies receive at most 70% of eligible costs; non-profit legal entities receive up to 100%.
- For-profit organisations: up to 70% of eligible costs, so at least 30% must come from their own resources
- Non-profit legal entities (for example universities and research organisations): up to 100% of eligible costs
- Co-financing conditions: the call sets no rule on cash or in-kind co-financing beyond the funding rate; the remainder is simply not reimbursed
Grants may not produce a profit: any surplus of revenue plus grant over costs is deducted from the final grant.
For lump sum grants the rate is applied when the lump sum is calculated and does not appear in the grant agreement.
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, General Annexes · pp. 31–32 · G — Form of grant, funding rate and maximum grant amount

cards.title: Budget constraints
cards.answer:
The grant is a lump sum fixed from a detailed budget table, which must still follow the normal cost-eligibility rules.
- Eligible costs: the detailed budget table must contain only costs that would be eligible under an actual-cost grant (personnel, subcontracting, purchases, other direct costs), because the lump sum must approximate the costs actually incurred
- Overheads and VAT: indirect costs are included in the lump sum calculation at the standard 25% flat rate of direct costs (excluding subcontracting)
- Subcontracting or equipment: purchases and subcontracting must give best value for money and be free of conflicts of interest; ineligible costs in the budget table can lead to a reduced grant, even late in the project
Payment depends on completing the work packages, not on proving the costs.
cards.sources:

funding_timing_submission.title: Timing
funding_timing_submission.question: What timing should the proposal submission and project follow?

cards.title: Application route
cards.answer:
Two stages (a short, anonymous outline first; only consortia that pass are invited to send a full proposal), through the EU Funding & Tenders Portal.
- Stage 1 — Outline proposal: 2 February 2027, 17:00 Brussels time; at most 10 pages, evaluated blindly, so organisation names, acronyms, logos and staff names must not appear in the abstract or Part B
- Stage 2 — Full proposal: 2 September 2027, 17:00 Brussels time, by invitation only after passing stage 1; Part B of at most 48 pages (the 45-page lump sum limit plus 3 pages for the business case and exploitation strategy), with a detailed lump sum budget table
- Opening: 13 October 2026, so the call is already open
- Additional procedure: none; the Commission may delay deadlines by up to two months

cards.title: Project window
cards.answer:
The call sets no duration or start date: both are fixed in the grant agreement.
- Maximum duration: not set by the call; the grant agreement states the duration in months, and extensions are possible only exceptionally
- Required start: normally after the grant agreement is signed; an earlier start is possible only exceptionally, for duly justified reasons and with the granting authority's agreement
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, General Annexes · pp. 30–31 · G — Starting date & project duration

cards.title: Decision and contracting
cards.answer:
Indicatively, stage 1 results come about 3 months after its deadline, and the grant is signed about 8 months after the stage 2 deadline.
- Expected invitation or assessment result: about 3 months after the stage 1 deadline (indicative)
- Funding decision: about 5 months after the stage 2 deadline (indicative)
- Grant agreement: about 8 months after the stage 2 deadline (indicative)
- Conditions before starting: an invitation to grant preparation is not yet a funding commitment, since legal entity validation, financial capacity and exclusion checks follow; the partners must sign a written consortium agreement

funding_timing_submission.title: Application
funding_timing_submission.question: Mandatory information to include in the application

cards.title: Mandatory submission package — pass/fail
cards.answer:
The proposal must be complete, submitted electronically before the deadline, and within the page limit; incomplete applications are rejected.
- Application form: Part A (administrative data and a summary budget, filled in online) and Part B (the technical description, uploaded as a PDF) through the EU Funding & Tenders Portal, using the forms inside the submission system; Part B is limited to 48 pages; the stage 1 outline is limited to 10 pages
- Budget: the summary budget in Part A and a detailed budget table, which is the basis for the lump sum
- Mandatory annexes: a plan for the exploitation and dissemination of results, including communication activities (not needed at stage 1), and the ethics self-assessment
- Partner documents: the coordinator confirms at submission that it has the mandate to act for all applicants; every participant signs a declaration of honour before the grant is signed
- Registration: every beneficiary, affiliated entity and associated partner needs a participant identification code (PIC, a number from the EU Participant Register) before submission; validation of beneficiaries follows at grant preparation
- Parallel submission: none
- Blind first stage: no organisation names, acronyms, logos or staff names in the stage 1 abstract and Part B
- Business case and exploitation strategy: required, backed by the companies' management, and decisive under the impact criterion
- Lump sum: the detailed budget table at stage 2 is used to fix the lump sum

cards.title: Evaluation and selection — scored or ranked
cards.answer:
Independent experts score three criteria out of 5; a proposal needs 3 on each and 10 in total, and Impact weighs 1.5 times in the ranking.
- Evaluation criteria: Excellence (clear, ambitious objectives beyond the state of the art; sound methodology), Impact (credible pathways to the expected outcomes; dissemination and exploitation measures) and Quality and efficiency of the implementation (work plan, risks, resources, capacity of each partner)
- Stage 1: only Excellence and Impact are scored, each needing at least 4; the overall stage 1 threshold is set so that about three times the budget goes through to stage 2, normally 8 or 8.5
- Thresholds: at least 3 out of 5 for each criterion and 10 out of 15 overall
- Weighting: for ranking, the Impact score counts 1.5 times
- Ranking rules: equal scores are separated first by whether a proposal covers aspects of the call not covered by higher-ranked ones, then by the Impact score, then Excellence, then gender balance among lead researchers and geographical diversity
- Budget assessment: the grant awarded may be lower than requested, and topic budgets may change by up to 20% after evaluation

cards.title: Conditional and exceptional requirements
cards.answer:
A blind first stage, a mandatory business case with 3 extra pages, a recommended emission-avoidance method and the lump sum are specific to this topic.
- Exception — blind evaluation: stage 1 proposals must be anonymous
- Exception — page limit: 3 extra pages at stage 2 for the business case and exploitation strategy
- Conditional — exploitation plan: as an output, an elaborated plan with feasibility study, business plan and financial model, naming funding such as the Innovation Fund, InvestEU and cohesion funds
- Conditional — scope: pure demand-side management is excluded
- Conditional — results transfer: the granting authority may object to transfers or exclusive licensing for 4 years after the project
- Recommended: a greenhouse-gas avoidance methodology with baselines and projected reductions, for example the Innovation Fund method
cards.sources: Horizon Europe Work Programme 2026–2027, Digital, Industry and Space · pp. 67–70 · HORIZON-CL4-2027-02-MAT-PROD-32-two-stage, Specific conditions and Scope
